script.opening: “Hello, it’s Daniel Cohen — Lionel Cohen’s son. Dad died on Monday morning. I’m sorry, I don’t really know who to ask. The certificate says heart failure, and there’s a medical examiner involved, and we still can’t register or bury him. In our religion we bury as soon as we can. What is going on?”

facts.text: If asked: Daniel, 52, the only son, named executor in the will. Lives 40 minutes away. His mother Ruth (Lionel’s wife) is with his aunt. Gives his father’s date of birth if asked (2 February 1945).

“Mum found him in his chair at about five in the morning. The paramedics came, said he’d died, and the police came briefly because it was at home — they said it wasn’t suspicious.” Dad had been more breathless for two weeks, “but he’s always breathless”.

“A medical examiner officer rang yesterday. She was very kind. She read out the cause and asked if we had questions. I said no — I was too upset. She said the examiner would sign it off and send it to the registrar. Nobody said when.”
If asked what he thinks it should say: “His lungs. He was on oxygen at night some of the time… I mean, he had inhalers and the nebuliser. He smoked for fifty years. Why does it say heart?”

Only if asked whether anything else is troubling him or about his father’s care: “Mum rang twice in the last fortnight for a home visit. Both times a doctor phoned instead and gave him antibiotics and steroids. Nobody came. If someone had seen him, he might still be here. I want to know why.”
If asked what he would like to happen: “I want to bury my father. And I want someone to look at what happened — but not if it means a post-mortem. We don’t do that unless we have to.”
Family is Jewish (United Synagogue). The burial society is waiting for the paperwork. “Every day is painful for Mum.”
Only if asked how he is coping himself: (long pause) “I hadn’t seen him for six weeks. We had a row about them moving into a home. I was going to go this weekend.” Voice breaks.
If asked about family: “Mum isn’t eating. She keeps saying she should have rung 999 that night. She’s 78, she’s got her own heart problems.”

Tired, polite, controlled anger underneath. Start with practical questions. If the doctor defends the practice (“the doctor followed protocol”) or dismisses the concern, become angry: “So nobody’s responsible?” If the doctor listens, says sorry for what the family is going through, and explains clearly how the concern can be looked at, calm down and say: “Thank you. That’s all I wanted — for someone to take it seriously.” Reveal the guilt only if asked about yourself. If the doctor explains honestly that raising a concern with the ME could involve the coroner, think aloud: “I don’t want to delay him… but I need to know.”

ice.ideas: “It was his lungs, not his heart — and he should have been seen.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he had not visited his father for six weeks after a row about a care home and feels intense guilt; some of his anger at the practice is guilt. He also worries his mother blames herself and is not coping. He shares this only if asked how he is coping.
ice.expectations: To understand the certificate and the delay, to get the funeral arranged quickly, and to have his concern about the home visits taken seriously — ideally without a post-mortem.

cues: “I don’t really know who to ask” — overwhelmed by an unfamiliar process.
“In our religion we bury as soon as we can” — faith needs and time pressure.
“He’s always breathless, but…” — a concern about care waiting to be invited.

checkpoints.text: Opens with sincere condolence, confirms who Daniel is (son, next of kin, executor), and checks he is able to talk — recognising that sharing relevant information with those close to a deceased patient is appropriate unless the patient had objected
Finds out what he already knows and what his questions are (the certificate wording, the medical examiner, the delay, the funeral) before explaining

Explains the MCCD clearly: part I is the sequence leading directly to death (heart failure due to ischaemic heart disease), part II lists conditions that contributed (COPD) — his lungs are recorded as part of the cause

Explains the statutory medical examiner system accurately (since 9 September 2024 all deaths not investigated by a coroner are independently reviewed; the ME looks at the records, speaks to the family and agrees the cause with the certifying doctor or notifies the coroner) and registration within 5 days, and offers to ask the ME office about timing given the family’s faith
Invites and listens to the concern about the home visits without interrupting or defending, and checks what outcome he wants

Responds honestly: says sorry for the distress (without speculating on fault), explains he can raise the concern with the ME (who may decide the coroner needs to be notified, which could affect timing), and that the practice will review the care, offer a meeting with the doctors, and explain the complaints route; does not promise an outcome
Asks how Daniel is coping, responds to his guilt with compassion, and asks about his mother — offering support for her (appointment, bereavement services)

Agrees concrete next steps (contact the ME office today, practice review and meeting, written information on bereavement and complaints), documents the conversation, and safety-nets for the family’s wellbeing

worked.txt: “I’m so sorry about your dad. Can I check — you’re his son, and you’re handling things for the family? Is now a good time to talk?”

“The certificate is written as a chain. The top line is what directly led to his death — his heart was failing, because of the narrowed heart arteries he’d had for years. His lungs are there too, in the second part, as something that contributed. So his COPD is recorded.”

“Since 2024, every death that doesn’t go to the coroner is checked by a medical examiner — an independent senior doctor who wasn’t involved in his care. It’s routine, not because anything is suspicious. They read the notes, talk to the family, and agree the cause with the GP before it goes to the registrar.”
“You mentioned he was breathless for two weeks. Is there anything about his care that’s troubling you?”

“I’m so sorry — that must be awful to carry. I can’t tell you today whether a visit would have changed things, but you deserve a proper answer, and we will look at it carefully. You can also tell the medical examiner. I should be honest: if they think the coroner needs to know, that could affect timing. It’s your right to raise it, and I’ll support you either way.”
“And how are you doing, in all this?” … “Arguments happen in families who love each other. It doesn’t change how much your dad meant to you.”

f.learning: Since 9 September 2024 the medical examiner system is statutory in England and Wales: any doctor who attended the deceased during life can complete the MCCD (the old 28-day rule has gone), and every death not investigated by a coroner is independently scrutinised by a medical examiner, who also speaks with the bereaved and can raise concerns or notify the coroner. Families usually need three things: a plain explanation of the certificate (part I is the causal sequence; part II contributing conditions), a clear picture of the process and timing (registration within 5 days, faith needs considered), and a safe place to raise concerns about care. Respond to concerns openly — listen, say sorry for the distress, explain the routes (medical examiner, practice review, meeting, complaint) honestly including the possible effect on timing — and look after the bereaved, whose anger often carries guilt.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: The Medical Certificate of Cause of Death Regulations 2024 and DHSC Guidance for medical practitioners completing MCCDs in England and Wales (September 2024, updated April 2025) · National Medical Examiner good practice guidance (NHS England) · Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019 · GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · GMC Good medical practice (2024) · Access to Health Records Act 1990 · NHS England Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (2022)
knowledge.summary: A bereaved son questions the MCCD, the medical examiner process and his father’s care. Explain the certificate and the statutory ME review, invite and handle the concern openly, and support the family.

points.t: Since 9 September 2024 any registered medical practitioner who attended the deceased during life can complete the MCCD if they can state the cause to the best of their knowledge and belief and the death does not need to be notified to the coroner. The 28-day rule no longer applies.

An independent senior doctor reviews the records and proposed cause of death, discusses it with the certifying doctor, and offers the bereaved a conversation — a chance to ask questions or raise concerns. The ME office then sends the MCCD to the registrar.

Under the Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019, deaths must be notified to the coroner if, for example, the cause is unknown, unnatural, violent, related to an injury or poisoning, or due to neglect or failure of care. The ME or attending doctor decides; a concern about care does not automatically mean a post-mortem.

Part I gives the chain of events leading directly to death (1a due to 1b due to 1c). Part II lists significant conditions that contributed but are not part of the chain. COPD in part II means it is recorded as contributing.

Deaths in England and Wales should normally be registered within 5 days. ME offices and coroners try to respond quickly where families have religious requirements for prompt burial; contact the ME office to explain.

Listen fully, acknowledge and say sorry for the distress (an apology is not an admission of liability), avoid speculating, explain routes: the ME conversation, a practice learning review (PSIRF), a meeting with the clinicians, the practice complaints procedure and the ICB or Ombudsman if needed. Apply the duty of candour if harm is found.

GMC (2017): the duty of confidentiality continues after death, but you can usually share information with those close to the patient to help them understand the death, unless the patient asked you not to. The personal representative can apply for records under the Access to Health Records Act 1990.
Ask about the caller and other family members; offer appointments, bereavement support (Cruse, faith-specific services such as Jewish Bereavement Counselling Service), and a follow-up call.

model.text: Hello Mr Cohen, it’s Dr Lee from the practice. I’m so sorry about your father. Can I check — you’re his son, and you’re handling things for the family? Is now a good time?
Yes. I’m the executor. The certificate says heart failure, there’s a medical examiner, and we still can’t bury him. In our faith we bury quickly. What’s going on?
That’s a lot to deal with on top of losing him. Let me take your questions one by one. What did the examiner’s officer tell you?
She read out the cause, asked if I had questions. I was too upset. Why heart? It was his lungs.

The certificate is a chain. The top line is what directly led to his death — his heart was failing, because of the heart disease he’d had since his heart attack. His lungs are there too, in the second part, as something that contributed. So his COPD is recorded.
model.why: Plain explanation of part I and part II

model.text: Since 2024, every death that doesn’t go to a coroner is checked by a medical examiner — an independent senior doctor. It’s routine. They read the notes, talk to the family and agree the cause before it goes to the registrar. I’ll ring the examiner’s office today to explain that you need to bury your father as soon as possible.
model.why: Accurate ME explanation and practical help with timing

model.text: Thank you. He was breathless for two weeks, though…
Is there something about his care that’s troubling you?
Mum rang twice for a home visit. Both times they phoned instead. Nobody came. If someone had seen him he might still be here.

I’m so sorry — that’s an awful thing to be carrying. I can’t tell you today whether a visit would have changed things, but you deserve a proper answer. We will look at his care carefully and I’d like to offer you and your mum a meeting. What would you like to happen?
model.why: Acknowledges, apologises for distress, asks desired outcome

model.text: I want someone to look at it. But not a post-mortem. We don’t do that unless we have to.

I understand. You can also tell the medical examiner — that’s part of their role. I should be honest: if they felt the coroner needed to know, that could affect timing; it doesn’t automatically mean a post-mortem. Our own review and a meeting will happen either way. It’s your choice and I’ll support you.
model.why: Honest about routes and consequences; respects his choice

model.text: And how are you doing, in all this?
(Pause.) I hadn’t seen him for six weeks. We argued about a care home. I was going this weekend.
I’m so sorry. Families who love each other argue — it doesn’t change what you meant to him. How is your mum?
model.why: Compassionate response to guilt; asks about mother

model.text: Not eating. She thinks she should have rung 999.

Please tell her I’d like to see her — I’ll ring her tomorrow. So: I’ll call the examiner’s office today about timing; you decide whether to raise your concern with them; the practice will review your dad’s care and offer a meeting; I’ll send details of bereavement support, including the Jewish Bereavement Counselling Service. If you or your mum feel unable to cope, call us or 111. I’ll write this conversation in his record.

social.t: Jewish and Muslim families usually seek burial as soon as possible and may object to post-mortem examination; less invasive options (such as post-mortem CT) may be available if the coroner investigates.
Anger at services often carries guilt about family conflict or missed chances; acknowledging both helps.
Older bereaved spouses have increased risk of illness and death in the following months; proactive contact is good practice.

legal.t: Statutory in England and Wales from 9 September 2024 (Medical Certificate of Cause of Death Regulations 2024).
Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019 list the circumstances requiring notification, including deaths possibly due to neglect or failure of care.
Personal representatives (or those with a claim) can apply for the deceased’s records under the Access to Health Records Act 1990.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) and the professional duty of candour: be open when things go wrong, apologise, explain and put things right.
Practices review deaths and concerns using PSIRF-style learning responses; involve the family in what is reviewed.
Record the call, the concern, the information shared and agreed actions; tell the certifying GP and the practice manager.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support, Jewish Bereavement Counselling Service, synagogue community, Age UK for the widowed spouse, GOV.UK “What to do when someone dies” and Tell Us Once.

redFlags: Bereaved family member not coping, not eating, or with thoughts of self-harm
A concern that may indicate a death needing coroner notification
psychosocial: Jewish faith — urgent burial, objection to post-mortem
Widowed mother with heart disease, self-blame
ice: Idea: his lungs, and he should have been visited
Expectation: explanation, prompt burial, concern taken seriously without a post-mortem

playbook.diagnosis: Bereaved son needing explanation of the MCCD and the statutory medical examiner process, with a concern about care (two declined home visits) and unspoken guilt.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The certificate shows his heart was the main cause, with his lungs contributing. The examiner check is routine, and your concern will be looked at properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to bury your dad quickly and you want to know his care was right — we can work on both.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge guilt; reach out to the widowed mother; faith-specific bereavement support.
sharedPlan: GP contacts ME office today about timing and faith needs
Daniel decides whether to raise the concern with the ME
Practice review of the home-visit requests; meeting offered to the family
GP to call Ruth tomorrow; bereavement support details sent
safetyNet: If Daniel or Ruth are not coping or have thoughts of self-harm — contact practice or 111

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by defensiveness, inaccurate information about the new death-certification process, or missing the family’s grief.

items.fail: “The doctor followed protocol — telephone triage is standard.”
items.why: Defensive; closes down a legitimate concern.
items.fix: Listen, say sorry for the distress, and offer a proper review.

items.fail: “The medical examiner is involved because something is suspicious.”
items.why: Inaccurate; the review is routine for every death not investigated by a coroner.

items.fail: Discouraging him from raising the concern to avoid delay.
items.why: Undermines his right to raise concerns and the ME’s role.
items.fix: Explain the routes and implications honestly; it is his choice.

items.fail: Promising “no post-mortem” or an outcome of the review.
items.why: Not the GP’s decision; false promises damage trust.
items.fix: Explain who decides and what you will do.

items.fail: Not inviting the concern at all.
items.why: He only raises it if asked; it would resurface as a complaint.
items.fix: “Is anything about his care troubling you?”

items.fail: Never asking how Daniel or his mother are.
items.why: Misses guilt and a vulnerable widowed spouse.

timeMap.d: Sorry for your loss; son, executor; good time to talk.
What he knows; part I chain and part II contributing — COPD recorded.
Routine statutory review; family conversation; registration within 5 days; GP to contact ME office about faith needs.
Invite; listen; sorry for distress; routes: ME, practice review, meeting, complaint; honest about coroner and timing.
Guilt; mother not eating; support; actions; documentation; safety-net.

wordPics.clearFail: Defends the practice or dismisses the concern; gives wrong information about the ME or certificate; no condolence or support.
wordPics.fail: Explains some of the process but does not invite or properly handle the concern, or makes promises about post-mortem or outcome.
wordPics.pass: Offers condolence, explains the MCCD and ME process accurately, listens to the concern, apologises for the distress and explains how it will be looked at.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: acts on the faith-related timing, is honest about the possible coroner route while respecting his choice, finds and responds to his guilt, reaches out to his mother, and agrees concrete documented actions.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: acts on the faith-related timing, is honest about the possible coroner route while respecting his choice, finds and responds to his guilt, reaches out to his mother, and agrees concrete documented actions.

avoid.dont: “The medical examiner is just a formality.”
avoid.instead: “It’s a routine independent check — and a chance for you to ask questions or raise concerns.”

avoid.dont: “A visit wouldn’t have made any difference.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t say today — but we will look at it carefully and talk it through with you.”

avoid.dont: “If you raise it, the funeral will be delayed.”
avoid.instead: “If the examiner felt the coroner should know, it could affect timing. It’s your right to raise it, and I’ll support you.”

Idea (it was his lungs; he should have been seen); concern (delay, guilt, his mother); expectation (explanation, quick burial, concern heard).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
